captions.linkedin:
Built an entire brand from nothing.

No brief. No identity. No product name. Just a dropship stainless steel cutting board sourced off a supplier page.

I named it KURA. Positioned it for home cooks who take kitchen hygiene seriously. Wrote the tagline ("Clean Surface. Clear Mind."), picked the palette (deep slate, warm cream, burnished copper), and built a three-font type system, display, serif, body, before writing a single line of HTML.

Then I built the homepage. It opens with a preloader that types the brand name in, then reveals: GSAP horizontal scroll on the use-case section, clip-path reveals on the brand imagery, a parallax hero, a marquee trust bar running on pure CSS, scroll-triggered fades on every section via IntersectionObserver. No external JS libraries.

The goal was never "nice website." It was making a product that costs $48 to source feel like it belongs next to brands spending millions on brand equity. That gap is design. It's copy. It's page speed. It's whether the above-the-fold gives someone a reason to keep reading.

Need a store like this built for your brand? That's what I do, DM me.

captions.linkedin:
Built a landing page for KURA, a stainless steel cutting board brand I made up. Concept build, not a client.

A landing page gets one visitor, from one ad, with one question in their head. Here it's "why would I swap my wooden board?" So the page answers that before it tries to sell anything.

How it runs, top to bottom:
✅ the claim and the button on the first screen: a board that doesn't hold bacteria
✅ the problem next. Knife grooves in wood and plastic trap stuff you can't scrub out
✅ then the board itself, and six reasons in plain tiles
✅ reviews, three steps, and the doubts people actually have (will it dull my knives? can it go in the dishwasher?)
✅ the guarantee sits right above the price, so the risk is handled before the button comes back

No nav menu. Nowhere to wander off to.

captions.linkedin:
Built an advertorial for KURA, a steel cutting board brand I made up. Concept build, not a client.

An advertorial has a different job from a product page. The reader came for an article, so the page has to read like one first and sell second.

How this one is laid out:
✅ a magazine masthead, a byline and a real headline about kitchen hygiene
✅ the problem gets three sections before the product shows up: knife grooves, bacteria, why plastic isn't the fix
✅ on desktop a small offer card rides along in the right rail, so the button is there when someone's ready without breaking the article
✅ then why steel, how the board works, and one reader's story
✅ the offer comes last, dark slate with the price and one copper button

The hard part with advertorials is patience. Sell too early and it reads like an ad, and people leave.
